subtype: Hopeful and apprehensive about the future [Regulating]
passage: Devika beta, you keep saying you can't sleep because of placement season, so let your Raghav chacha tell you about 1994. I was twenty-one, in my final year at the polytechnic in Nashik, and every night I'd lie awake, half dreaming of a job in Bombay, half sure I'd fail every interview and disappoint my father. Hope in one hand, dread in the other, and both too heavy. One evening my lecturer, Mr Sathe, found me staring at the notice board. He didn't give a speech. He said, "Write down five companies. Next to each, one thing you can do this week." So I did: one letter, one mock interview with him, one visit to a senior who worked at a factory in Satpur. Small things. The dread didn't vanish, but now it had something to hold. I didn't get my first choice. I got the third, and that's where I met your chachi, so no complaints.

qa.q: Where did Raghav Chacha study?
qa.a: At the polytechnic in Nashik.

qa.q: What was young Raghav feeling during those sleepless nights?
qa.a: He felt hopeful about a job in Bombay and, at the same time, full of dread about failing and disappointing his father.

qa.q: What turning point helped young Raghav manage the dread?
qa.a: Following Mr Sathe's suggestion to list five companies with one small step each that week, such as a letter, a mock interview and a visit to a senior.

qa.q: How might Mr Sathe have seen young Raghav at the notice board?
qa.a: As a worried student who needed practical steps more than a speech, which is why he offered a simple plan.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult facing placements with both hope and dread, and turning vague dread into manageable action through small steps and a mentor.

subtype: Bored and tired in study life [Expressing]
passage: You asked why I'm suddenly awake in Thermodynamics, Madhuri. Honestly? I'm Pradeep, and last semester I was a mess. In every lecture I'd yawn so wide my jaw clicked, fill the margins with doodled robots, and scroll my phone under the desk. Professor Nair once stopped mid-sentence and asked if the class was keeping me up. I blamed the lectures; they were dull, sure. But the truth was I was sleeping at three every night, gaming or watching videos, then running to an eight o'clock class. Bored and exhausted looked exactly the same on me, and I couldn't tell which was which. So I tried an experiment for three weeks: phone in the drawer at midnight, a ten-minute walk between the two morning lectures, and notes in a grid so my hands had something to do besides robots. The lectures didn't get more exciting. But I stopped yawning, and I understood entropy for the first time. Mostly, it was sleep.

qa.q: What did Pradeep doodle in the margins?
qa.a: Robots.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling in those lectures?
qa.a: Pradeep felt bored and exhausted at once, the two blurring together because of sleeping at three every night.

qa.q: What did Pradeep's three-week experiment include?
qa.a: Phone in the drawer at midnight, a ten-minute walk between the morning lectures, and grid notes to keep the hands busy.

qa.q: How might Professor Nair have read Pradeep's yawns?
qa.a: As a sign that the lecture was boring Pradeep, which is why the professor asked, half-joking, if the class was keeping Pradeep up.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult showing yawns, doodling and phone use in lectures, where boredom and tiredness overlap, and structure, breaks and rest help.

passage:
Sunday night
Lunch at Samir's grandparents' house in Lucknow. Five hours of my best behaviour. I sat with my back straight, ankles crossed, and said "ji" so many times it stopped sounding like a word. When his cousin told the story of the goat at the wedding, I wanted to laugh so badly, but his Dadi wasn't laughing, so I pressed my lips together and smiled politely. When his uncle asked about my job, I gave short, careful answers. It was respect, and I'd do it again; that's how you meet elders the first time. But by four o'clock my face ached from holding it. In the car Samir said, "You were so quiet. Were you okay?" I finally laughed, the big loud laugh I'd been saving since the goat story. "I was being polite! It's exhausting." He said next time I could slip out to the garden with his sister, where nobody minds loud laughing.
Payal

qa.q: What story did Samir's cousin tell?
qa.a: The story of the goat at the wedding.

qa.q: How did Payal feel by four o'clock?
qa.a: Payal felt tired and strained, face aching from holding back reactions, even though the restraint felt respectful.

qa.q: What could make the next visit less draining?
qa.a: Taking a break in the garden with Samir's sister, where loud laughter is fine, while still showing respect to the elders.

qa.q: How did Samir read Payal's quietness?
qa.a: He worried Payal might not be okay, not realising it was polite restraint.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult keeping reactions muted with a partner's elders as a sign of respect, and finding that constant restraint is tiring.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
subtype: Bodily signs are not lie detectors [Interpreting]
passage:
Monday: A phone went missing from the hostel common room, and the warden called everyone in. When she asked Maria whether she'd been there after dinner, Maria went red to her ears, her hands trembled on the chair back, and a line of sweat appeared on her lip. Akash, watching from the back, thought: well, that's obvious. By evening he'd told two friends his theory.
Wednesday: Maria sat alone in the mess. Akash overheard her telling her roommate, "I blush when anyone even looks at me. Being questioned in front of everyone was a nightmare." She'd been on a call with her mother in the corridor the whole time.
The following Monday: The phone turned up. A visiting cousin of another student had picked it up by mistake. Akash found Maria at the notice board. "I thought it was you because you went red. I told people. I'm sorry." Maria looked at him for a long moment. "Thanks for saying it. Please tell them too."

qa.q: Where had Maria been during the time in question?
qa.a: On a call with her mother in the corridor.

qa.q: What might Akash have felt when the phone turned up?
qa.a: Akash likely felt guilty and ashamed for blaming Maria and spreading the theory, which is why he apologised.

qa.q: What could Akash have done differently on Monday?
qa.a: Treated the blushing, trembling and sweating as signs of stress that innocent people show too, and kept his guess to himself.

qa.q: What was it like for Maria to be suspected because she blushed?
qa.a: Lonely and hurtful: she sat alone in the mess, and being questioned in front of everyone was already a nightmare for her.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult wrongly reading blushing, trembling and sweating as guilt, and learning that these reactions occur in innocent people and are never proof.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
subtype: Trembling and sweating before high-stakes events [Regulating]
passage: In the corridor outside the practical exam hall at the nursing college in Kolar, Ishita's hands would not stop shaking. Her palms were so damp she wiped them on her white coat twice. "I'm going to drop the thermometer," she whispered. Nirmala, a final-year student volunteering that day, sat beside her on the bench. "Your heart's racing because your body's getting ready," she said. "It's the same feeling as excitement. Tell yourself, 'I'm ready,' not 'I'm scared.'" She showed Ishita how to press both feet into the floor and name five things she could see: the peeling green paint, the fan, the notice about bus timings, a crow on the window, her own name on the list. Ishita's breathing slowed. "Does it ever stop?" she asked. "Mostly it gets smaller," Nirmala said. "If it ever turns into panic that won't settle, even on ordinary days, the college counsellor is good. I went in my second year." Then Ishita's name was called.

qa.q: How many things did Nirmala ask Ishita to name?
qa.a: Five things she could see.

qa.q: What was Ishita worried about in the corridor?
qa.a: Ishita felt anxious that her shaking hands would make her drop the thermometer in the exam.

qa.q: Which tools did Nirmala offer?
qa.a: Reframing the racing heart as readiness, pressing the feet into the floor, naming five things in sight, and the counsellor if panic ever keeps coming back.

qa.q: How did Nirmala seem to see Ishita's nerves?
qa.a: As a normal sign of the body getting ready, something Nirmala had felt too, not a weakness.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult with shaky hands and damp palms before a practical exam, easing it with grounding and reframing, with professional support for persistent panic.

subtype: Direct versus indirect communication across cultures [Mismatch]
passage:
In their Bengaluru hostel room, Harsha looked up from a book. "It's quite cold tonight, no?"
Chaitanya didn't look up from the laptop. "Yeah, December."
"Hmm. The window's letting in a lot of wind."
"Mm-hmm."
Harsha pulled the blanket up to the chin and sighed.
Chaitanya finally looked up. "Wait. Are you asking me to close the window?"
"Only if you don't mind. I didn't want to be rude; it's your side of the room."
"Oh! You can just say 'please close the window.' I'd never have guessed."
"At home, if I said it that straight, Amma would say I was ordering people around."
"And at mine, if you hint, nobody notices. My family just says things."
"So what do we do?"
"You try saying it plainly. And if you go quiet and sigh, I'll ask, 'Is there something you'd like?'"
"Okay. Then, please close the window."
Chaitanya closed it, grinning. "See? Nobody died."

qa.q: Which month is it?
qa.a: December.

qa.q: Why did Harsha hint instead of asking directly?
qa.a: Harsha felt uncomfortable being blunt, worried it would seem rude since the window was on Chaitanya's side and plain requests sounded like ordering people around at home.

qa.q: What agreement did they reach?
qa.a: Harsha would try saying needs plainly, and Chaitanya would ask kindly whenever Harsha went quiet or sighed.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya experience Harsha's hints?
qa.a: As ordinary small talk; Chaitanya missed the request at first because in Chaitanya's family people just say things.

grounding: It illustrates a direct speaker and an indirect speaker learning that neither style is better and that kind clarifying questions bridge the gap.

passage:
Outside the photocopy shop, Binita caught up with Rekha. "You snapped at the photocopy uncle just now. That's not you."
"I'm fine."
"You've said 'I'm fine' for five weeks. You look exhausted. You answer everything in two words."
Rekha was silent for a long moment. "Papa's been in and out of hospital since August. I do the nights with him, then come to college. I can't remember the last time I slept properly."
"Five weeks of that. No wonder."
"I thought if I just pushed through the semester..."
"What if you didn't do it all alone? Could your brother take two nights a week?"
"He's offered. I kept saying no."
"Say yes. And the college counsellor has evening slots. Would you go if I walked you there tomorrow after lab?"
"...Okay. I'll message my brother tonight."
"And right now you're napping in the library reading room while I copy your notes."
Rekha laughed for the first time in days. "Bossy."
"Caring. Same thing."

qa.q: Since when has Rekha's Papa been in and out of hospital?
qa.a: Since August.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling behind the short answers and snapping?
qa.a: Exhaustion and strain from five weeks of nights caring for Papa on top of college, feelings Rekha had been hiding behind "I'm fine".

qa.q: Which steps did Binita suggest?
qa.a: Accepting the brother's offer of two nights a week, visiting the college counsellor together, and a nap in the reading room right away.

qa.q: How had Binita been seeing Rekha over those weeks?
qa.a: As not like Rekha at all: tired-faced, curt and snapping, which worried Binita enough to name the pattern.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult carrying weeks of stress that shows as a tired face, short answers and irritability, and a friend steering them toward rest, support and counselling.

passage:
Friday, results day
I've just realised Aadhya thinks I didn't care. When the scholarship list went up on the notice board this morning, I found my name third from the top, and my whole chest went electric. I wanted to scream. Instead my face did what it always does when something is huge: nothing. I read it twice, nodded, and walked back to the bench. Aadhya was bouncing. "Hafsa! You got it! Why aren't you jumping?" I said, "Yeah, it's good." She looked at me as if I'd commented on the weather. Later I heard her tell someone, "She didn't even seem happy." But inside I was shaking. I think my blank face is how I hold things still enough not to spill over, especially in public. Ammi does the same. At home tonight I cried and laughed at once, and Ammi hugged me for ages. Tomorrow I'll tell Aadhya what was really going on behind my face.
Hafsa

qa.q: Where was Hafsa's name on the list?
qa.a: Third from the top.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling while her face stayed blank?
qa.a: Hafsa was hugely excited and shaky inside, chest "electric", holding it still so as not to spill over in public.

qa.q: What could Hafsa do so that Aadhya doesn't misread the blank face again?
qa.a: Tell Aadhya, as Hafsa plans to, what was happening behind it, and perhaps put the feeling into words in the moment next time.

qa.q: How did Aadhya read Hafsa's reaction?
qa.a: As indifference; Aadhya thought Hafsa didn't care or wasn't happy about the scholarship.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult keeping a flat face on results day while feeling great excitement inside, and others wrongly assuming indifference.

subtype: Speaking politely while angry in formal settings [Regulating]
passage: I was next in the queue at the phone company's service centre, so I heard all of it. The young woman ahead of me, Sonali according to the token screen, had been charged twice for the same month, and this was her third visit. Her jaw was tight and her knuckles were pale around a folder of printouts. But her voice stayed low and polite. "I understand it's not your fault. I've been here three times. I'd like this reversed today, in writing, please." The clerk started on the usual script. Sonali waited, then repeated, just as calmly, "In writing, today, please." The clerk fetched a supervisor, who stamped a letter within ten minutes. Outside, I saw her meet a friend, Anirban, and the moment they turned the corner she let out a sound halfway between a growl and a laugh and stamped her foot twice. He laughed and handed her a cold drink. I can't know what she felt inside, but it looked like anger finally finding its way out.

qa.q: How many times had Sonali visited the service centre?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What did Sonali's tight jaw and pale knuckles suggest?
qa.a: She was likely angry and frustrated after three visits, while keeping her voice low and polite.

qa.q: What made Sonali's request effective?
qa.a: She stayed courteous, didn't blame the clerk, and calmly repeated a clear, specific request, reversed today and in writing, until a supervisor acted.

qa.q: How did Anirban respond when Sonali let off steam?
qa.a: He laughed and handed her a cold drink, giving her anger a safe, friendly outlet.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult staying courteous while frustrated in a service dispute, making a calm firm request, and releasing the anger afterwards.
